title: How would you prevent replay attacks in an API Gateway (nonce, dedupe within a time window via Redis)?
shortTitle: How to prevent replay attacks in an API Gateway

s1_definition.profdef: A replay attack is when an attacker captures a legitimate, already-authenticated request and sends it again to trigger the same action a second time, such as repeating a money transfer. The gateway prevents it by making each request provably one-time-use. The standard mechanism is a unique nonce per request plus a timestamp, with the request signed so they cannot be altered; the gateway rejects any request whose timestamp is outside a short freshness window and rejects any nonce it has already seen, tracking seen nonces in a fast shared store like Redis with a time-to-live equal to the window. Together, freshness and single-use defeat replay.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh signs a cheque to pay rent and hands it over. A replay attack is someone photocopying that cheque and cashing it again and again. To stop this, National Bank of India stamps every cheque with a unique serial number and the exact time it was written. The teller refuses any cheque older than a few minutes, that is the freshness window, and keeps a short list of serial numbers already cashed, so the moment a photocopy with a seen serial number shows up, it is rejected. The serial number is the nonce, the stamped time is the timestamp, and the teller's short list lives in Redis.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make every request single-use and fresh, meaning a signed unique nonce plus a timestamp, reject stale timestamps outside a short window, and reject any nonce already recorded in Redis with a TTL equal to the window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A replay attack is when an attacker captures a legitimate, already-authenticated request and sends it again to trigger the same action a second time, such as repeating a money transfer. The gateway prevents it by making each request provably one-time-use. The standard mechanism is a unique nonce per request plus a timestamp, with the request signed so they cannot be altered; the gateway rejects any request whose timestamp is outside a short freshness window and rejects any nonce it has already seen, tracking seen nonces in a fast shared store like Redis with a time-to-live equal to the window. Together, freshness and single-use defeat replay.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh signs a cheque to pay rent and hands it over. A replay attack is someone photocopying that cheque and cashing it again and again. To stop this, National Bank of India stamps every cheque with a unique serial number and the exact time it was written. The teller refuses any cheque older than a few minutes, that is the freshness window, and keeps a short list of serial numbers already cashed, so the moment a photocopy with a seen serial number shows up, it is rejected. The serial number is the nonce, the stamped time is the timestamp, and the teller's short list lives in Redis.

**One line to remember:** Make every request single-use and fresh, meaning a signed unique nonce plus a timestamp, reject stale timestamps outside a short window, and reject any nonce already recorded in Redis with a TTL equal to the window.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand why authentication alone does not stop replay. A valid JWT proves the caller's identity, but if an attacker captures a complete valid request, including its token, they can resend the exact bytes and the gateway will see a perfectly valid token and accept it again. So replay protection is a separate concern layered on top of authentication.

The core idea is to make each request unique and fresh. Uniqueness comes from a nonce, a number used once, which the client generates randomly per request, for example a UUID. Freshness comes from a timestamp the client includes. To stop an attacker from simply changing the nonce or timestamp, these fields must be covered by a signature or an HMAC, so tampering invalidates the request. The gateway verifies the signature first; if it fails, the request is rejected before any replay check.

The freshness check is the first filter. The gateway compares the request timestamp to the current time and rejects anything outside a short window, for example five minutes, accounting for reasonable clock skew. This bounds how long a captured request could even be replayed and, importantly, bounds how many nonces the gateway must remember, because a nonce older than the window can never be accepted anyway.

The dedupe check is the second filter and the heart of the defense. The gateway must remember which nonces it has already processed and reject repeats. It stores each seen nonce in a fast, shared store, which is why Redis is the standard choice: it is fast enough to check on every request, and it is shared across all gateway replicas so a request replayed to a different replica is still caught. The crucial technique is an atomic set-if-absent. In Redis this is `SET nonce 1 NX EX 300`, which sets the key only if it does not already exist and expires it after three hundred seconds. If the command reports the key was set, this nonce is new and the request proceeds; if it reports the key already existed, this is a replay and the request is rejected. Using the atomic NX avoids a race where two copies of a replayed request both pass a separate "check then set".

The TTL ties the two filters together. Because the freshness window already rejects anything older than five minutes, the nonce only needs to be remembered for that same five minutes, after which it expires automatically. This keeps the Redis memory bounded no matter how many requests flow through, because nonces are constantly aging out.

A senior nuance is scope. Replay protection should be applied to state-changing, non-idempotent operations, like transfers and payments, not to safe reads, because adding a nonce to every GET is wasteful and reads are naturally safe to repeat. Another nuance is idempotency keys, which solve a related problem from the client's own retries: a client that legitimately retries a transfer after a timeout sends the same idempotency key, and the server returns the original result instead of charging twice. Replay protection and idempotency keys look similar but differ in intent, one defends against attackers, the other makes honest retries safe, and a well-designed system often uses both. A final nuance is that the Redis dedupe store is now a shared dependency on the critical path, so it must be highly available, and you decide the failure policy deliberately: fail closed, rejecting requests if Redis is down, is safer for money movement than fail open.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An attacker sits on a compromised network and captures Rajesh's legitimate, fully authenticated request to transfer fifty thousand rupees to Priya. The token is valid, the body is valid, everything is valid. The attacker resends the exact request five times, hoping to drain Rajesh's account by repeating the transfer. Authentication cannot stop this because every copy is genuinely authenticated.

Problem 2 — The bank runs several gateway replicas behind a load balancer, so the attacker's replayed copies might each land on a different replica. A per-replica in-memory "seen" list would fail, because replica A does not know what replica B has seen. We need a shared store.

The connection to the fix: we will build a replay guard that requires each transfer request to carry a nonce and a timestamp, rejects stale timestamps outside a freshness window, and records seen nonces in a shared store using an atomic set-if-absent with a TTL. The demo simulates Redis with a shared map and shows the first transfer succeeding while the four replays are rejected, including one sent to a "different replica".

What the code will do. There is a `SignedRequest` carrying the user, amount, nonce, timestamp, and a signature flag. There is a `ReplayStore` modeling Redis `SET NX EX` with TTL expiry. There is a `ReplayGuard` that verifies the signature, checks freshness, and dedupes the nonce atomically. There is a `TransferGateway` that only executes the transfer if the guard allows it. The demo sends one genuine transfer, four exact replays, one replay to a second guard instance sharing the same store, and one request with a stale timestamp.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one genuine transfer and several attacker replays, plus a stale and a tampered request, across two gateway replicas sharing one store.

Step 1. The genuine transfer arrives at replica A. Its signature is valid, so it passes the first check. Its timestamp is now, well inside the five-minute window, so it passes freshness. Its nonce has never been seen, so the atomic set-if-absent succeeds and records the nonce with a five-minute TTL. The guard allows it and the transfer executes once.

Step 2. The attacker replays the exact same request to replica A four times. Each copy has the same valid signature and the same still-fresh timestamp, so it passes the first two checks. But the atomic set-if-absent now reports the nonce already exists, so each of the four is flagged as a replay and rejected. The transfer never executes again.

Step 3. The attacker sends the same request to replica B, hoping a different replica has not seen it. But replica B's guard uses the same shared store, so the set-if-absent again finds the nonce present and rejects the request as a replay. This is exactly why the dedupe store must be shared, like Redis, rather than per-replica memory.

Step 4. A request with a timestamp ten minutes old arrives. Its signature is valid, but the freshness check computes an age beyond the five-minute window and rejects it as stale before even touching the nonce store. This also illustrates why the nonce TTL can safely equal the window: a request this old could never be accepted anyway.

Step 5. A tampered request arrives whose signature does not verify. The guard rejects it at the very first check, because without a valid signature nothing about the nonce or timestamp can be trusted. Only correctly signed, fresh, never-before-seen requests execute, which is exactly the replay-proof behavior we wanted.

```
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [INFO] === Genuine transfer (first time) ===
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [INFO] EXECUTE transfer user=rajesh amount=50000 nonce=7f3a1b2c
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [INFO] === Attacker replays same request 4x (to replica A) ===
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [SEVERE] REJECT: replay detected nonce=7f3a1b2c
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [SEVERE] REJECT: replay detected nonce=7f3a1b2c
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [SEVERE] REJECT: replay detected nonce=7f3a1b2c
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [SEVERE] REJECT: replay detected nonce=7f3a1b2c
2026-10-24 14:00:01 [INFO] === Attacker replays to a DIFFERENT replica (shared Redis catches it) ===

  POST /transfers  {user, amount, nonce, timestamp, signature}
    │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
            ▼
   Shared Redis (all gateway replicas) ── nonce auto-expires after window
   Replica A sees nonce → Replica B rejected too (shared state)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A replay attack is when an attacker captures a legitimate, already-authenticated request and simply sends it again to make the same thing happen twice, like repeating a money transfer. The key insight is that authentication alone does not stop it, because the captured request carries a perfectly valid token, so the gateway would see a valid request and accept the replay. Replay protection is therefore a separate layer on top of authentication, and its job is to make every request provably single-use and fresh.

I achieve this with three things working together. First, every state-changing request carries a unique nonce and a timestamp, and both are covered by a signature or HMAC so an attacker cannot tamper with them. The gateway verifies that signature first. Second, the gateway enforces a short freshness window, rejecting any request whose timestamp is older than, say, five minutes, which bounds how long a captured request could even be replayed. Third, and most importantly, the gateway dedupes the nonce: it remembers which nonces it has already processed and rejects any repeat.

The dedupe store is where Redis comes in, and the technique matters. In my banking work at National Bank of India, we run several gateway replicas behind a load balancer, so an attacker's replayed copies can land on different replicas. A per-replica in-memory list would fail, because one replica would not know what another had seen. So we use Redis as a shared store and record each nonce with an atomic set-if-absent command, Redis `SET nonce value NX EX 300`, which sets the key only if it does not already exist and expires it after the same five minutes as the freshness window. If the command reports the key was newly set, the nonce is fresh and the transfer proceeds; if the key already existed, it is a replay and we reject it. The atomic NX is essential, because it closes the race where two copies of a replay could both slip through a separate check-then-set. And because the freshness window already rejects anything older than five minutes, the nonce only needs to live in Redis for those five minutes, so the memory stays bounded as nonces age out.

The nuances I always raise are scope, idempotency, and the failure policy. I apply replay protection only to state-changing operations like transfers, not to safe reads, because reads are naturally fine to repeat. I also distinguish replay protection from idempotency keys: replay protection defends against an attacker, while an idempotency key makes an honest client's own retry safe by returning the original result instead of charging twice, and a good system uses both. Finally, because the Redis dedupe store now sits on the critical path, it must be highly available, and for money movement I deliberately fail closed, meaning if Redis is unreachable I reject the request rather than risk letting a replay through.
